Lessons.Title: Nearest Multiples of 10 and 100
ExplanationParagraphs: This lesson compares a whole number with its enclosing multiples of 100 and of 10. The mathematically nearest multiple is determined by distance, not by naming a convenient benchmark; the teacher also reviews the representations that make the distance visible.

Warm-up (10 min). The original 2021 page shows an unlabeled point somewhere between 100 and 200 on a 0–200 number line. Pupils make too-low, about-right and too-high estimates. Because the original figure pixels have not been recovered and verified, do not assign an exact value or auto-grade these estimates.

Activity 1 (20 min): locate 128, 272, 436, 89 and 351 on hundred-interval number lines. The source asks for the nearest hundred and then the nearest ten. Record the enclosing tens first for 128: 120 and 130, with 130 nearer because 128 is 2 from 130 and 8 from 120.

Source values and first-party mathematical checks: 128 -> 100 and 130; 272 -> 300 and 270; 436 -> 400 and 440; 89 -> 100 and 90; 351 -> 400 and 350. The first result in each pair is the nearest multiple of 100; the second is the nearest multiple of 10.

Activity 2 (15 min): explain how 349 is nearer 300 than 400 but nearer 350 than 340; 712 is nearer 700 than 800 but nearer 710 than 720; 568 is nearer 600 than 500 but nearer 570 than 560. Compare actual distances, then explain how place value lets you do the comparison without plotting.

Apply to the original numbers 324 (nearest hundred 300, nearest ten 320) and 89 (nearest hundred 100, nearest ten 90). These numeric anchors can be checked independently; a teacher must still review source-number-line construction, oral reasoning, the unrestricted estimate and the unverified publisher Cool-down.

The five 100-wide number-line templates and one warm-up picture described by the archive are only alt-text/source-link evidence. No claim is made to copy publisher drawings or prove pixel parity. This independent text and teaching proposal has not passed Stage D or live Rich V2 verification.

KeyConcepts.Title: Enclosing multiples of 100
KeyConcepts.Definition: The neighboring multiples of 100 on either side of a number.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For 272, compare 200 and 300 using the distances 72 and 28.

KeyConcepts.Title: Enclosing multiples of 10
KeyConcepts.Definition: The neighboring multiples of 10 on either side of a number.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nearest and rounding
KeyConcepts.Definition: Round to the nearest requested place by choosing the nearer benchmark.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare both endpoint distances. At an exact midpoint, a stated rounding convention is needed.
KeyConcepts.Example: 351 is nearer 400 than 300, but nearer 350 than 360.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number-line evidence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Relative position can justify which of two benchmarks is nearest.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Locate the number accurately on an interval with correct scale; discuss placement with a teacher.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two nearest benchmarks for 128
WorkedExamples.Question: From the source list, find both nearest hundred and nearest ten for 128.
Steps: 128 lies between 100 and 200: it is 28 from 100, 72 from 200.
128 lies between 120 and 130: it is 8 from 120, 2 from 130.
The closer hundred is 100; the closer ten is 130.
WorkedExamples.Check: 128 rounds differently at the two place values.

WorkedExamples.Title: The contrast in 349
WorkedExamples.Question: Which benchmark is nearer to 349: 300 or 400? 340 or 350?
Steps: Explain why the two choices measure different scales.
WorkedExamples.Check: The place value changes the benchmark interval.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mentally round 568
WorkedExamples.Question: For source number 568, which hundred and ten are nearest?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use number place value and verify with distances.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both checks use strict smaller distance.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source exit examples
WorkedExamples.Question: What are the nearest hundred and ten to 324 and 89?
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not treat the tens answer as a hundreds answer.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use the nearest ten when the task asks for the nearest hundred.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The reference benchmarks differ by place value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label which place value is requested before selecting endpoints.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choose 300 for 351 because the first digit is 3.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check distance to the next hundred; 400 is nearer.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Give only 130 for 128 without naming its surrounding tens.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original source asks pupils to identify and compare the two enclosing tens.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify 120 and 130, compare 8 and 2, and justify 130.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the warm-up estimate and drawing quality as an integer auto-grade.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original point's exact position and pupils' justifications require the original picture and teacher feedback.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep warm-up and drawing tasks teacher-reviewed.

SummaryPoints: For nearest hundred, compare neighboring multiples of 100; for nearest ten, compare neighboring multiples of 10.
A number line shows a reason, not just a rounded integer; independent numeric checks do not certify teacher-observed work.
Source PDF, original figure geometry/pixels and publisher Cool-down remain unverified; status is A_C_EXPLICIT_GAP.
